considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), lt), 5))), RANK(SUB(RANK(RATIO(sstk, at)), RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity-heavy financing is bearish when earnings-plus-depreciation coverage of liabilities is deteriorating.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), RATIO(re, at)))), RANK(SUB(RANK(RATIO(prstkc, at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)))))

considered.name: External Funding After Dividend Stop
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dvc, at), 1))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))))
considered.hypothesis: External financing is bearish when weak-cash-flow firms cut dividends.
considered.reasoning: This removes the lagged near-duplicate structure and isolates a cleaner dividend-distress channel rather than broad payout retrenchment. A dividend cut combined with weak cash generation and outside financing is a stronger sign of funding stress than either the cut or financing action alone.

considered.name: Quality Failed Reborrower
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 5)), RANK(MIN(RATIO(LAG(dltr, 1), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(dltis, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Reborrowing after prior debt retirement is bullish when operating cash-flow quality is improving.
considered.reasoning: This addresses the wrong-way slope concern by reversing the economic interpretation: reborrowing after paydown may be benign or growth-oriented when cash flow is improving. The signal tests whether the same financing sequence is informative in the opposite direction for high-quality improving firms rather than assuming it is always distress.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: Internally consistent and economically coherent, but it is essentially a rank-product of two canonical anomalies (cash-based operating profitability and net share issuance/payout), so the multiplicative form loads heavily on the known main effects and must be shown to add something beyond a simple additive composite.

Sign logic is correct (high composite = low quality plus heavy issuance → negative slope) and the retained-earnings conditioning on issuance is a defensible refinement, though both ingredients (RE/assets quality, equity issuance) are well-documented and the smoothed-earnings/RE SUMRANK is largely redundant with itself.

This is a near-mechanical product of two of the most-published anomalies (the accrual anomaly, since oancf−ib is negative accruals, and net external financing of Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan) and is also substantively the same quality×payout template as the first proposal, offering little incremental information.

Debt retirement intensity conditioned on a cash-flow trend is a genuinely less-explored financing angle with consistent sign logic, but dltr is sparsely populated and the ratio is unstable for low-debt firms, so coverage and portfolio-composition diagnostics must be checked.

The expression matches the hypothesis and the expected negative sign, and combining current-ratio liquidity with cash generation as a conditioner on debt issuance is a reasonable distress-financing refinement rather than a restatement of the plain net-debt-issuance anomaly.

GROWTH(csho,1) is contaminated by splits and stock dividends unless adjusted (e.g., by ajex), making the "dilution" leg partly mechanical noise, and the remaining content is a straightforward share-issuance × profitability-trend crossing mislabeled as a "novel" interaction.

This is essentially profitability × the debt-issuance/net-external-financing anomaly (Spiess–Affleck-Graves, composite issuance), and it re-runs the same profitability-confirmed-deleveraging mechanism as the archived "Cash Flow Recovery Deleverager" with only the debt-reduction proxy and quality proxy swapped, so it is closer to a coverage patch than a new economic hypothesis.

The conditioning leg is copied verbatim from the archived "Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress," but the action leg (debt maturity-structure shift rather than gross issuance) is a genuinely distinct and under-mined construct, though it is noisy because a large long-term debt repayment mechanically raises the score without implying rollover stress.

This is a cosmetic variant of the archived "Gross Profit Deterioration Security Issuer" — same deteriorating-gross-profitability × issuance mechanism with only the scaling denominator changed from assets to sales and dltis dropped — so it does not test a substantively new channel.

Internally consistent and a real reframing of the failed dividend-cut idea (payout increase confirmed by high *and* low-volatility operating cash flow), though the mechanism sits close to well-known dividend-signaling and cash-flow-volatility effects and coverage will be limited to dividend payers with a large mass of zero changes.

The indicator construction is logically coherent but produces a degenerate distribution — roughly 80% of firms score exactly zero, so quantile portfolios and the FMB slope are driven entirely by one flagged subset — and the underlying claim that cash-burning external-finance-dependent firms underperform is already well documented (Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan external financing, distress/profitability screens).

The MIN() co-occurrence operator to capture simultaneous borrowing *and* distribution is a genuinely novel construction rather than a reweighting of either anomaly alone, the sign logic matches the expression, and the debt-funded-payout-under-weak-cash-flow mechanism is economically specific and not a standard published factor.

The MIN-based dual-market issuance requirement is a genuinely different financing construct from the archive's additive `sstk+dltis` version, though the conditioning leg is copied verbatim from Low Quality Equity Recapitalizer, so the incremental information is modest and it risks loading on the same net-external-financing anomaly.

critic_notes.target_name: Low Gross Quality Debt Funded Buyback
critic_notes.rationale: This is a cosmetic variant of the archive's best performer, Weak Cash Debt Funded Payout (fmb -3.64, ls_talpha -3.97) — identical MIN(debt issuance, payout) structure with oancf swapped for gross profit and dividends dropped — so it will be highly correlated with an already-evaluated signal rather than testing a new mechanism.

Replacing cash-flow volatility with cash-flow acceleration is a substantive shift from dispersion to directional deterioration and is internally consistent with the negative expected sign, but it reuses the identical financing leg from the failed Unstable Cash Financing Spike and ACCEL of an annual ratio is a noisy second difference, so the improvement odds are only moderate.

Near-rediscovery of Gross Profit Deterioration Security Issuer — same NEG(TREND(x/at,5)) × issuance structure, with sale/at mechanically nested inside gross-profit/at (which equals sale/at times gross margin) — so it is a minor decomposition of an already-tested signal rather than a new channel.

Substituting the liquidity *trend* for the level and requiring co-occurrence (MIN) of long-term issuance with short-term debt growth is a defensible restructuring of Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress, and the sign logic holds (DELTA(dlc) negative correctly pushes deleveragers to the bottom), though dropping the oancf term discards the leg most likely responsible for the prior version's alpha.

The construction is internally coherent and the MIN(buyback, debt reduction) requirement is a real refinement over the archive's crude buyback confirmation, but it is close to the sign-flipped complement of Weak Cash Debt Funded Payout and every long-side quality-payout variant in the archive has produced negligible FF5 alpha, so the prior for economic significance is low.

The conditioning leg is byte-for-byte the same as archived "Weak Cash Dual Issuer" and "Low Quality Equity Recapitalizer," with only the second MIN argument swapped from dltis to dvc, making this a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism — and since dvc/at is typically an order of magnitude smaller than sstk/at, the MIN will almost always collapse to dividend intensity, so the "equity-funded" framing is not what the expression actually measures.

Using the year-over-year *change* in dollar net equity issuance interacted with persistent weak OCF is a genuinely different (flow-acceleration rather than level) dimension from the archived level-based issuance/buyback interactions and the sign logic is internally consistent, though it is close to the known net-share-issuance anomaly and the DELTA of a scaled flow will be noisy.

The conditioning term is identical to archived "Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress," so any result risks being driven by the already-tested leg, but MIN(dltis, dltr) as gross rollover churn (as opposed to net issuance) is a substantively new construct worth one test — with the caveat that gross debt churn is mechanically size- and maturity-structure-driven and may proxy for revolver accounting rather than distress.

dp/sale introduces a genuinely new conditioning variable not present anywhere in the archive and the sign logic is coherent, but it is layered additively onto NEG(MA(oancf/at,3)) — the exact leg that drove the archive's strongest result — so the design cannot separate incremental information in maintenance burden from the known cash-flow effect, and dp/sale is heavily industry-determined.

This is effectively a relabeling of the archived "Retained Earnings Dilution Trap" (lt/at and NEG(re/at) are near-mechanical substitutes since retained earnings is the dominant swing component of book equity) and, more broadly, a direct rediscovery of the well-documented distress-plus-equity-issuance anomaly.

The combination of current-ratio *level* with a short-term-debt-and-dividend co-occurrence MIN is distinct from the archived liquidity-*trend* × debt-layering and OCF × payout signals, and the sign is consistent, though the MIN behaves oddly when Δdlc is negative (it simply reverts to a debt-paydown rank) and dvt/at has limited cross-sectional dispersion among payers.

This is the archive's "Weak Cash Net Equity Reversal" with the already-tested `NEG(SUMRANK(oancf/at, act/lct))` conditioner from "Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress" bolted on — a mechanical recombination of two existing archive components rather than a new mechanism.

It is a two-component parameter swap (level→change in dividends, level→trend in cash flow) on the archive's "Equity Issuer Unsupported Dividend," and the change-based payout leg also introduces a sign inconsistency, since dividend *cuts* at weak-cash issuers now rank as bullish despite the archive's opposite prior.

The distinctive and rare `MIN(dltis, -Δdlc)` term-out trigger leg is identical to the already-evaluated "Quality Liquidity Term Out," so with the same sparse coverage the result will be dominated by the same firm-months and only the quality conditioner is genuinely new — a refinement, not a substantively different signal.

The economic idea (financing amid sales-cash divergence) is reasonable and distinct from the archive's gross-profit-trend version, but subtracting un-normalized trends of `sale/at` (level ≈1) and `oancf/at` (level ≈0.1) means the conditioner is numerically dominated by the sales-turnover trend, so the signal likely proxies improving turnover × issuance and its natural direction contradicts the stated negative sign; rank-standardize each trend before differencing.

This is a direct rediscovery of "Low Quality Refinancing Treadmill" with identical inputs and only SUMRANK replaced by a product of the two conditioner ranks — a purely cosmetic reformulation with near-identical cross-sectional ordering.

Weak-retained-earnings × equity-issuance has already been tested twice in the archive ("Retained Earnings Dilution Trap," "Low Retention Equity Financing"), both times producing long-short alphas of the *wrong* sign, and adding the already-tried `VOL(oancf/at,5)` conditioner does not address that diagnosed failure.

This is effectively a rediscovery of the archive's "Weak Cash Net Equity Reversal" (repurchase-to-issuance switch conditioned on weak cash flow) built from two already-tested legs — NEG(TREND(oancf/at,5)) and MIN(sstk, prstkc) — with only a LAG added, so it is a cosmetic recombination rather than a new mechanism.

The sequential equity-then-debt "financing escalation" ordering is a genuinely new twist on the archive's contemporaneous dual-issuer test, though both component legs (NEG(MA(ni/sale,3)) and MIN(sstk, dltis)) are recycled, so incremental information is limited.

The MIN() conjunction is internally incoherent because it compares a financing *level* (typically 0.02–0.10 of assets) with a payout *change* (typically near zero), so the signal will almost always collapse onto the payout-cut term and simply reproduce the archive's "Cash Deterioration Payout Withdrawal" (fmb −3.73) rather than test the stated financing interaction.

This is a minor variant of the archive's "Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress" that swaps the cash-flow *level* leg for a cash-flow *volatility* leg, precisely the substitution that already produced a wrong-signed, insignificant result in "Unstable Cash Financing Spike," so it re-tests a discredited component without a new economic argument.

Redirecting the working maintenance-burden conditioner from debt issuance to equity issuance is a defensible new channel test, but the construction is thin (a two-way interaction whose second leg is the well-known share-issuance anomaly) and dp/sale largely proxies capital intensity, so the marginal contribution over the existing dp/sale signals is modest.

A product of two volatility measures contains no directional financing information and will mostly proxy for idiosyncratic volatility/size and lumpy small-firm issuance, and the VOL(oancf) leg has already delivered wrong-signed results in the archive, so the negative expected sign is not well supported by what the expression actually computes.

This is a mechanical debt-side clone of the already-tested "Weak Cash Net Equity Reversal" (identical quality leg, financing flow swapped), and it embeds a noisy second difference (DELTA of DELTA(dlc)) that muddies the "net borrowing change" interpretation.

Beyond being a MIN→SUB cosmetic variant of "Quality Liquidity Term Out," the maturity leg subtracts a change (DELTA(dlc)) from a gross level (dltis), so the term is dominated by long-term debt issuance scale rather than any maturity shift, contradicting the stated hypothesis.

(dp − oancf)/at is essentially a re-parameterization of the already-tested "Maintenance Burden Debt Issuer" quality leg and is dominated by the negative-cash-flow component, making this yet another weak-cash-flow × debt-issuance screen already represented several times in the archive.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquidity Weak Debt To Equity Escalation
critic_notes.rationale: The ordered debt-then-equity escalation channel is a genuinely distinct hypothesis from the archive's contemporaneous-co-occurrence screens, though the MIN-of-gross-flows construction and low expected coverage repeat a design pattern that has performed erratically here.

This is a legitimate diagnosis-driven repair of the earlier signal's pathological MIN over a sign-changing debt delta rather than a purely cosmetic tweak, but it reuses the same three ingredients so the incremental information content is modest.

This is effectively the known composite external-financing anomaly conditioned on cash-flow quality, and it duplicates several archive entries (e.g., "Liquidity Weak Debt Funding Stress," "Own History Funding Strain") with only a change of cash-flow scaler from at to lt.

This is a cosmetic re-parameterization of the archive's already-strong "Weak Cash Debt Funded Payout" (same weak-cash-flow conditioner and same debt-plus-payout interaction, with MIN swapped for a rank product and levels swapped for TS_RANK), so it tests no new economic mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Weak Margin Debt To Equity Rescue
critic_notes.rationale: The expression is a straightforward recombination of two archived signals — the margin conditioner from "Weak Margin Financing Escalation" and the LAG(dltis)→sstk ordering (with identical hypothesis wording) from "Liquidity Weak Debt To Equity Escalation" — and merely reversing the issuance order plus lagging the deflator is too incremental.

Internally consistent and the (ib+dp)/lt coverage ratio is a legitimately different distress conditioner, but the archive already tested this exact MIN(dltis, dltr) churn interaction with two separate quality conditioners, making this a third conditioner swap rather than a new mechanism.

Structurally identical to the archived "Ranked Short Debt Dividend Strain" with only the payout variable changed from dividends to repurchases; the discretionary-vs-sticky payout distinction is a real economic difference but too small a step to justify a fresh test, especially since the parent's fmb_tstat was ~0.

This is a direct mashup of two archived signals — "External Funding Payout Retrenchment" with its cash-flow-trend term replaced by the NEG(GROWTH(sale,1)) term from "Demand Slump Debt Issuer" — i.e., a variable substitution rather than a substantively different hypothesis.

Signs and construction are coherent and the asset-growth-versus-sales-growth productivity gap is a genuinely different conditioner from the archive's cash-flow-quality family, though it sits close to the canonical asset-growth and net-external-financing anomalies and the two legs are mechanically correlated (issuance funds asset growth), so the incremental content over plain asset growth needs to be demonstrated.

This is close to a cosmetic re-scaling of the archived "Current Obligation Debt Issuer" (lct-based strain × dltis/at), differing only in using a one-year change in lct/sale instead of a level relative to cash capacity, and the family of "weak-condition × debt issuance" interactions has already been mined repeatedly with weak fmb support.

The construct is a variable-swap on the archived triple-product "Ranked Short Debt Dividend Strain"/"Liquidity Squeeze Dividend Borrower" (cash conversion replacing the current ratio, short-debt share replacing the short-debt level change), and those variants already showed the diagnostic pathology of decent ls_talpha with a null Fama-MacBeth slope, which this proposal does nothing to address.

It reuses verbatim the MIN(sstk/at, -Δdebt/at) equity-financed-deleveraging leg from the archived "Low Quality Equity Recapitalizer" (fmb -0.74, alpha ≈ 0) and merely swaps the conditioner to sales growth, which overlaps the already-tested "Forced Deleveraging Demand Slump," so the expected incremental information is minimal.

The peak-to-current gross-profitability drawdown is a genuinely different functional form from the archived TREND-based version (level distance vs slope, so it identifies materially impaired firms rather than mildly declining ones), though it inherits the same issuance leg and does not directly attack the reason that signal's strong fmb slope failed to translate into portfolio alpha.

The equity-versus-debt financing-mix spread conditioned on cash-flow coverage of total liabilities is a coherent pecking-order/debt-capacity-exhaustion mechanism that is not in the archive (which only paired the coverage term with debt retirement), and the expression's direction correctly matches the negative expected sign.

The lagged-retirement-then-issuance sequencing is a substantively different dynamic from the archived contemporaneous refinancing-churn MIN(dltis, dltr) construct, but the sales-growth conditioner duplicates "Demand Slump Debt Issuer" and the MIN of two small scaled flows will likely yield a sparse, unstable long-short leg.

This is the ninth instance of the archive's exhausted "quality-deterioration × (sstk+dltis)/at" template — differing only in the conditioning variable, which itself (rising current assets relative to sales) is essentially the well-known working-capital-accrual/net-operating-asset anomaly, and the near-identical "Working Capital Equity Reliance" already tested a lct/sale variant.

This is a cosmetic level-to-trend substitution on the archived "Low Coverage Forced Paydown" (same NEG(coverage) conditioner, identical dltr/at financing leg), and the bearish-debt-retirement premise also runs against the standard net-debt-issuance anomaly direction without any new argument for why paydown should be bad.

Quality-conditioned buyback signals were already tested twice in the archive ("Persistent Cash Profit Buyback Confirmation," "Quality Deleveraging Buyback"), both with essentially zero FF5 alpha, and the only change here is swapping the net-repurchase leg for a rank-spread against total external financing — a recombination rather than a diagnosis of why the long leg failed.

The financing-mix spread (debt reliance versus equity reliance) is a substantively different construct from the archived maintenance-burden × issuance-level signals, and the archive's counterintuitive positive alpha on high-dp/sale equity issuers gives a coherent reason to expect the debt-minus-equity tilt to price negatively — though the proposal should have stated that diagnosis explicitly.

This is a near-duplicate of the archived "External Funding Payout Retrenchment" (identical three legs) with a one-period LAG applied to the payout-change term, which is a cosmetic timing tweak rather than a new mechanism.

The signal simply splices the conditioner from "Low Coverage Forced Paydown" onto the exact MIN(lagged dltr, dltis) financing leg from "Failed Deleveraging Reborrower" — a mechanical recombination of two archived signals, and the parent's Fama-MacBeth slope pointed the wrong way, which this proposal does not address.
